entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), founded in 1861 in response to the American Industrial Revolution by William Barton Rogers, is the world's leading research university for science, engineering, and technology — producing more Nobel laureates, Turing Award winners, and billion-dollar technology companies than any comparable institution. MIT's 97 Nobel laureates, 26 Turing Award winners, and alumni who founded companies worth $1.9 trillion (equivalent to the world's 10th-largest economy) have made it the single most economically productive university in history.

Rogers founded MIT on the principle of 'mens et manus' ('mind and hand') — explicitly rejecting European pure-science academic traditions to combine research with practical application. The move to Cambridge across the Charles River from downtown Boston in 1916 enabled campus expansion; the invention of modern architecture under Alvar Aalto and I.M. Pei's iconic Stata Center created a campus where buildings are intellectual statements. MIT's Lincoln Laboratory (radar), Instrumentation Laboratory (Apollo guidance computer), and Media Lab (wearable computing, e-ink) created the research spin-off model that made Silicon Valley possible.

The MIT-Stanford technology corridor is the template for the entire global technology startup ecosystem. MIT alumni founded Hewlett-Packard, Texas Instruments, Qualcomm, Intel, McDonnell Douglas, and Dropbox. The MIT OpenCourseWare initiative (2002) — placing the entire undergraduate and graduate curriculum online free — revolutionized global educational access. MIT's AI lab, founded by Marvin Minsky and John McCarthy in 1956, created artificial intelligence as a formal academic discipline.
